display_title: Meaningful but straightforward results, lack of techinical novelty

content.title: Meaningful but straightforward results, lack of techinical novelty
content.review:
This paper theoretically proves that gradient descent with Polyak’s momentum achieves a faster convergence rate than vanilla GD, on sufficiently wide one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

Comments:

>The theory developed in the paper partially confirms the common belief among practitioners that Polyak’s momentum helps neural network training, which is an encouraging result. I say “partially confirms” because the provable acceleration is only on very wide over-parameterized neural networks, while it is still unclear for relatively narrow networks. 

> Given the knowledge/results obtained in the NTK literature, this result is straightforward and not surprising. As shown by prior NTK works (e.g., [Jacot et al 2018, Lee et al 2019, Liu et al 2020]), when the network is sufficiently wide, it is approximately a linear model, which is recently termed as “transition to linearity” by [Liu et al 2020]). As is already clear, Polyak’s momentum accelerates in the linear model setting. Hence, it is also expected that it accelerates in this “approximate” linear setting. Note that the work [Du et al 2018] is essentially the same as the NTK analysis.

> The techniques used in the paper is a straightforward combination of Polyak’s analysis and the analysis in [Du et al 2018]. Since the wide networks are approximately linear, there is no technical difficulty to apply the Polyak’s analysis for linear models to the very wide networks.

> The paper does not show acceleration of Polyak’s momentum on networks with practical sizes (the result is on very wide ones). This is inconsistent with the claim in the paper title.

Overall, although the result is meaningful and should be respected, the theory is straightforward and lacks technical novelty. So, I don’t think this paper meets the standard of this conference.

References:

[Jacot et al 2018] Neural tangent kernel: Convergence and generalization in neural networks. NeurIPS 2018

[Lee et al 2019] Wide neural networks of any depth evolve as linear models under gradient descent. NeurIPS 2019

[Liu et al 2020] On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01092

[Du et al 2018] Gradient descent provably optimizes over-parameterized neural networks.  https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02054

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank you for your feedback. We have some thoughts regarding your comment.

*** === 1. "As is already clear, Polyak’s momentum accelerates in the linear model setting'' === ***

We respectfully don't agree with this. A model being linear does not necessarily mean that applying Polyak’s momentum to train the model will lead to acceleration. In fact, (Lessard et al. 2016) construct a function that is strongly convex but not twice differentiable for which Polyak’s momentum fails to converge. In the convex world, the class of smooth, strongly convex, and twice differentiable problems is the only known example that Polyak’s momentum provably has an acceleration. 

Furthermore, there is little positive result regarding Polyak’s momentum in non-convex optimization, as we described in the section of related works. We are not aware of any theoretical result of Polyak’s momentum showing an acceleration in non-smooth and non-convex optimization problems, compared to vanilla gradient descent.

The references that the reviewer listed were already mentioned and cited in this paper except [Liu et al 2020. "On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant''], which was on arXiv at the time of the ICLR submission deadline. Their theoretical results only apply to smooth activation. Hence, they are not applicable to ReLU.



*** === 2. "technical novelty'' === ***


The reviewer appears to be suggesting that our results are simply an "A + B = C'', where A is the analysis of Polyak momentum on quadratic problems that leads to acceleration, and B is the work of Du et al. 2019 which shows that gradient descent converges linearly in the NTK regime when training an over-parameterized network. We would like to respectfully but strongly disagree with this. The additional technical contribution to ensure that an accelerated rate is achievable in the NTK regime was significant and, we believe, particularly surprising. We required a number of subtle techniques in order to achieve the final result.


While it may appear to be straightforward, that is because we aimed to make our analysis as transparent as possible. While the appendix lays out a long and careful analysis, as a theory paper we wanted the main body to be simple, transparent, and easy to follow. The one-page sub-section (Subsection 3.2) is there to provide a more high-level intuition behind the central theory result. 


In that subsection, we give a high-level analysis to show that with over-parametrization, the residual dynamic of the neural training is not very different from the case given in Subsection 2.1 where Polyak's momentum is known to have acceleration.  We note that in the classical result, which we described in Subsection 2.1, the dynamic is about how the model parameters $\in R^d$ evolve, whereas, in analyzing training a ReLU network, the dynamic is about how the predictions $\in R^n$ evolve. We establish a connection between these two, and this connection has not been shown elsewhere, to our knowledge. As we mentioned in the introduction, prior to our work, there is only an asymptotic convergence result regarding Polyak's momentum (Krichene et al., 2020) under the mean-field limit.


It will be unfortunate and discouraging if the transparency of our analysis instead makes our result perceived as a straightforward one. We note that Reviewer 3 seems to approve our writing and encourage the practice of transparency for writing a theory paper.


*** === 3. "The paper does not show acceleration of Polyak’s momentum on networks with practical sizes" === ***


The condition of the network size is aligned with those GD convergence results in the NTK regime (e.g. Du et al. (2019b); Arora et al. (2019); Song and Yang (2019) and more). We explicitly mentioned (Du et al. 2019b) and compare the results in the abstract, so for readers who are familiar with the literature, our setting should be clear at the moment when they read the abstract. 

We also want to point out that even for vanilla gradient descent, there is little global convergence result regarding networks with ``practical sizes''. Asking our result to be improved to "practical sizes'' might be too much for this work, given the current progress in the literature. 


*** === 4. "I don’t think this paper meets the standard of this conference.'' === ***

 It would be helpful if the reviewer can let us know in what ways we could improve the results in this paper in order to meet this standard. Although we understand this is somewhat of a subjective question, other reviewers appear to disagree with this evaluation (R3 says "The topic (optimization for neural nets) is technical and fits well with ICLR'').

content.title: Response to the feedback
content.comment:
I thank the reviews for providing the detailed feedback. However, I would like to clarify a few things below:

Response to your point #1 above: As I mentioned, the Polyak acceleration is clear in the LINEAR model setting. I mention the linear model because the very wide network is almost a linear model, as shown in (Jacot et al, 2018; Lee et al 2019, Liu et al 2020). Note that I am not talking about other general convex functions. Clearly, the function constructed by (Lessard et al. 2016) is not a linear model.

About technical novelty: Talking about the lack of novelty in the review, I am not referring to the intuition in Subsection 3.2, transparancy of your presentation or the length of your proof. As I mentioned in the review, the proved acceleration of Polyak is basically the consequence of the "transition to linearity" of wide neural networks (Liu et al 2020) and the well known Polyak acceleration for linear models. The main proof idea of the paper is essentially following this strategy. To me, there is no very much new techniques introduced in this submission. Please provide specific techniques that you think are novel. 

About practical sizes of networks: I know that to analyze networks with practical sizes is really non-trivial, and I am also not expecting the authors to really have a theory for these networks. But your statements (especially in the title) should be consistent with your analysis results. Adding a word "wide" before network should be good. Otherwise, it is very misleading for readers who don't familiar with the literature. 

Response to your point #4: The paper is not strong in technical novelty, and the results are somehow straightforward. I don't think it meets the standard.

content.title: Thanks for the feedback of Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. We know that the output function of a neural net trained in the NTK regime can be approximated by a linear model. But this does not say too much about the optimization landscape of the network. To apply an existing acceleration result of Polyak's momentum, one has to characterize the optimization landscape of the underlying problem. To our knowledge, all the existing results of the accelerated linear rate of Polyak's momentum need at least a property that is similar to the strong convexity. Yet, solely having the strong convexity is not enough to show an accelerated linear rate of Polyak's momentum (e.g. [Ghadimi et al. 2015] and [Lessard et al. 2016]). 

[Liu et al. 2020b] establish a connection between solving an over-parametrized non-linear system of equations and solving the classical linear system. Drawn from this connection, they show that for smooth and twice differentiable activation, the optimization landscape of  an over-parametrized network satisfies a notion called Polyak-Lokasiewicz (PL) condition:

$
\frac{1}{2} \\| \nabla L(w) \\|^2 \geq \mu ( L(w) - L(w_*)),
$

where $w_*$ is a global minimizer and $\mu > 0$.  However, it is not very clear if their result can be extended to ReLU. (Safran et al. 2020) show that for a one-layer ReLU network in the student-teacher setting, the PL condition does not hold even locally after any degree of over-parametrization of the student network. Furthermore, to our knowledge, there is little theoretical result of Polyak's momentum showing an accelerated rate when an optimization landscape satisfies the PL condition but has more than one global minimum. On the other hand, for a problem that satisfies PL and has a unique global minimizer, (Aujol et al. 2020) show a variant of Polyak's momentum method having an accelerated rate in a continuous-time limit. So it is not clear if the result is applicable to our setting.

Our analysis does not follow (Liu et al. 2020a), as it requires smooth and twice differentiable activation and that their results build heavily on characterizing the spectral norm of the Hessian. Also, existing Polyak's acceleration results focus on analyzing the distance between $\\| w_t - w_* \\|$, where $w_*$ is the unique global minimizer of the underlying problem. However, analyzing the distance becomes tricky in our problem. It is not clear if one can show the Hessian of the over-parametrized ReLU network $W_t$ is actually positive definite (as the matrix $A$ on (5) in the paper) nor even properly define it. It is neither clear if the update of Polyak's momentum for the over-parametrized ReLU, $W_t \in R^{d \times m}$, can be well written as the form (5). We neither know which point the update will converge to.

To avoid these difficulties, our analysis focuses on analyzing how the predictions due to Polyak's momentum evolve over time, which is new compared to the existing analysis of Polyak's momentum. We have to carefully decompose the dynamic of the network's predictions due to momentum. As the dynamic is more complicated than that of vanilla GD, we have to switch back and forth the two equivalent presentations of gradient descent with Polyak's momentum to simplify the analysis. With this subtle effort, we were able to establish the acceleration result, which was lacking in the literature. 

We thank the reviewer for the fruitful discussion, which we believe does help to improve the presentation of our work.

Ref:

[Liu et al. 2020a] Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, and Mikhail Belkin. On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant. arXiv:2010.01092, 2020a

[Liu et al. 2020b] Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, and Mikhail Belkin. Toward a theory of optimization for overparameterized systems of non-linear equations: the lessons of deep learning. arXiv:2003.00307, 2020b.

[Ghadimi et al. 2015] Euhanna Ghadimi, Hamid Reza Feyzmahdavian, and Mikael Johansson. Global convergence of the heavy-ball method for convex optimization. ECC, 2015

[Lessard et al. 2016] Laurent Lessard, Benjamin Recht, and Andrew Packard. Analysis and design of optimization algorithms via integral quadratic constraints. SIAM Journal on Optimization, 2016.

[Aujol et al. 2020] Jean-Francois Aujol, Charles Dossal, and Aude Rondepierre. Convergence rates of the heavy-ball method with lojasiewicz property. hal-02928958, 2020.

[Safran et al 2020] Itay Safran, Gilad Yehudai, and Ohad Shamir. The effects of mild over-parameterization on the optimization landscape of shallow relu neural networks. arXiv:2006.01005, 2020.

display_title: Good paper, well written, but moderate the claim (convergence up to a neighborhood)

content.title: Good paper, well written, but moderate the claim (convergence up to a neighborhood)
content.review:
This paper proves theoretical guarantees for training a one hidden layer relu neural network with gradient descent+Polyak's momentum, a common practice among practitioners. This problem was only studied from an asymptotic point of view, i.e. without convergence rate. More precisely, the main result (Theorem 2) states that the outputs of the network converge linearly up to a neighborhood to the labels on the training set. This assumes that the step size, the momentum parameter, the number of nodes of the network and the number of features are set accordingly. Moreover, the linear rate is accelerated compared to that of gradient descent, in the sense that is it (1-\sqrt{\kappa}) instead of (1-\kappa). To my knowledge, proving theoretical guarantees for Polyak's momentum over GD is a difficult topic. Even for minimizing strongly convex functions, Polyak's momentum has provable advantage over gradient descent only in some particular cases.



Overall, it is a good paper that proves that for reaching a neighborhood of the solution, Polyak is faster than GD (based on the upper bounds provided by Th1 and Th2). The topic (optimization for neural nets) is technical and fits well with ICLR. The paper also provides nice intuitions, based on explaining how Polyak accelerates for quadratic problems, to explain why it is true. More generally, the paper is well written (some minor typos below) and easy to follow. The main theorem is proven in the main paper and some intuitions are given, which I believe is a good thing for a theoretical paper. Hence, there are no numerical experiments (not necessary in my opinion).
However, Th2 has some flaws even if it is a good entry point to understand neural networks training via Polyak's momentum. 


Theorem 2: First, the values of the parameters could be better explained. For instance, it is written \eta = O(\lambda/n^2) and later on \eta \lambda < 0.5. Moreover, there is a small discussion after the Th2 to explain the value of the parameters, but it can be improved. For instance, the authors could discuss the role of overparametrization. I don't see why the error is controlled by the number of neurons.
More importantly, Th2 proves convergence **up to a neighborhood** at an accelerated rate. In particular, the algorithm is not proven to converge to the labels. More discussion should be provided w.r.t. this point and the main claim of the paper should be moderated. On the contrary, gradient descent does converge (linearly). One way to answer this is to provide a complexity result: If I want to have error \le \varepsilon and I can set the parameters as I wish, what is the minimum number of iterations needed to achieve \varepsilon accuracy. I think that this number of iterations will be higher than the one of GD. 





MINOR:

Check third line of paragraph 2.1 and first sentence of page 5
Two lines before Eq 10: Notation = undefined
Section 3.1. Recall that S_i is a random set
Lemma 2: A_ir and S_i already defined
Three lines after Eq 34: sum symbol over r is missing several times.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We want to thank you for thoroughly reading the paper and for the encouraging feedback. We also appreciate your support of our technical presentation.

*** === 1. step size === ***

We thank the reviewer for the concern. We have an update of our result because Reviewer 4 pointed out a related work of vanilla GD (Wu et al. 2019b) showing that a larger step size $\eta= \frac{1}{c_0 \lambda_{\max}(\bar{H}) }$ is possible, where $\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H})$ is the largest eigenvalue of the Gram matrix $\bar{H}$ and the quantity $c_0>0$. 


With this in mind, we came to realize that our result does not require the step size $\eta$ to be $\eta = O(\frac{\lambda}{n^2})$ as in Du et al. 2019b. Our step size can be as large as

$
\eta = \frac{1}{2 \lambda_{\max}(\bar{H} )},
$

without hurting the analysis.

The new step size $\eta = \frac{1}{2 \lambda_{\max}(\bar{H} )}$ is at worst $\eta = O( \frac{1}{n} )$, because $\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H})$ can be bounded as  $\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H}) = \Theta (n)$ (Wu et al. 2019b). The change we made in the analysis for the update is minimal. We only edited one line in the main proof of our theorem on the main text. By using the large step size $\eta = 1 / (2 \lambda_{\max} (\bar{H}) )$, the constraint $\eta \lambda \leq \frac{1}{2}$ that was originally stated in the theorem is trivially satisfied, since $\lambda := \lambda_{\min} (\bar{H}) $.


Our new result is summarized as follows. Kindly find the update in the paper.

Let us denote the condition number of the Gram matrix $\bar{H}$ as $\kappa := \frac{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H}) }{ \lambda_{\min}(\bar{H}) }$.
By using the large step size $\eta = 1 / (2 \lambda_{\max} (\bar{H}) )$,
we show that with the help of momentum, the error decays at a rate

$\left( 1 - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\kappa}}  \right)$

to a small neighborhood.

We believe this is quite an interesting improvement for the following reason: the rate $\left( 1 - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\kappa}}  \right)$ matches that of the accelerated rate for optimizing strongly convex smooth problems (e.g. Nesteorv 1983;2004), and in this case the accelerated rate has an optimal dependency on the condition number $\sqrt{\kappa}$ instead of $\kappa$. On the other hand, the rate of vanilla gradient descent with the optimal step size (Wu et al. 2019b) is $  \left( 1 - \frac{1}{c' \kappa} \right)$ for some potentially large quantity $c'>0$. Our result hence shows the clear advantage of the use of Polyak's momentum.


*** === 2. "moderate the claim" === ***

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion.
We have stated that Polyak's momentum helps the convergence to a small additive error in quite a few places (e.g. abstract, the end of introduction, and the remark below the theorem). We now add the following sentence to the paper, let us know if this is not sufficient:

``In other words, Polyak's momentum helps to converge at an accelerated rate **up to** an $O(\frac{1}{n^\nu} \\| u_0 - y \\|)$ factor. While $\nu$ can be tuned to decrease this additional factor, this is at the expense of more neurons in the hidden layer.''

***  === 3. iteration complexity === ***

We had a comparison of iteration complexity (how many iteration is required to have a certain error). We now make another pass to polish the discussion in the paper, which we also show below. We hope the update helps to make the comparison clear.  

To analyze the number of iterations required to have an $\epsilon$ error, without loss of generality, we can assume that $\epsilon = \gamma \\| u_0 - y\ \|$for some number $\gamma \in (0,1)$. According to Theorem~1 (Du et al. (2019b)), vanilla gradient descent has

$
\\|
u_{t} - y 
\\| \leq \left( 1 - \frac{\eta  \lambda}{2} \right)^{t/2}
\cdot
\\|
u_{0} - y 
\\|.
$

Therefore, for the error $\\|u_t - y \\|$ to decrease to $\gamma \\| u_0 - y \\|$
for some number $\gamma \in (0,1)$,
vanilla gradient descent needs a number of iterations
$T^g_0 := \lceil \frac{ 2 \log \big(  \gamma   \big)}{ \log \big( 1 - \frac{\eta \lambda}{2} \big) } \rceil$.  

On the other hand, our result of gradient descent with Polyak's momentum shows

$
\\|
\begin{bmatrix}
u_{t} - y   \\\\\
u_{t-1} - y 
\end{bmatrix}
 \\|
\leq \left( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\eta  \lambda}{2}} \right)^{t}
\cdot 
\\|
 \begin{bmatrix}
u_{0} - y \\\\\
u_{-1} - y
\end{bmatrix}
\\| + \frac{ 1 }{2 \sqrt{2} n^\nu } \\| u_0 - y \\|
$

So gradient descent with Polyak's momentum takes a number of iterations
$T^m_0 := \lceil \frac{ \log \big(  \gamma /  (2 \sqrt{2}) \big)}{ \log \big( 1 - \sqrt{ \frac{\eta \lambda}{2} } \big) } \rceil$  for the error $\\| u_t - y\\|$ to decrease to $\gamma \\| u_0 - y \\|$.

content.title: continued (response to reviewer 3)
content.comment:
To see the iteration complexity, let $\frac{ 1 }{2 \sqrt{2} n^\nu } \\| u_0 - y \\| = \frac{\gamma \\| u_0 - y \\|}{2}$ on the r.h.s. of the inequality. Then, the number iterations for the term $
\\|
\begin{bmatrix}
u_{t} - y \\\\\
u_{t-1} - y 
\end{bmatrix}
\\| \leq \left( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\eta  \lambda}{2}} \right)^{t}
\cdot 
\\|
 \begin{bmatrix}
u_{0} - y \\\\\
u_{-1} - y
\end{bmatrix}
\\|
$ to decrease to $ \frac{\gamma \\| u_0 - y \\|}{2} $ is $\lceil \frac{ \log \big(  \gamma /(2\sqrt{2}) \big)}{ \log \big( 1 - \sqrt{ \frac{\eta \lambda}{2} } \big) } \rceil$.  

Consequently, the number of iterations requires for gradient descent with Polyak's momentum is only a fraction of what vanilla gradient descent needs, 

$
T^m_0 \lesssim  \frac{ \log\big( 1 - \frac{\eta \lambda}{2} \big) }{ \log \big( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\eta \lambda}{2}} \big) } T^g_0.
$

(A technical remark: we have $| 2 \log \gamma | \geq | \log (\gamma/(2\sqrt{2})) )|$ when $\gamma \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$. That is, the absolute value of the numerator of $T^g_0$ is larger than that of $T^m_0$ when $\gamma \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$  and it makes sense that we want $\gamma$ to be as small as possible.  Moreover, we have $\frac{ \log\big( 1 - \frac{\eta \lambda}{2} \big) }{ \log \big( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\eta \lambda}{2}} \big) } < 1$. This should demonstrate the advantage of Polyak's momentum.)

*** === 4. the role of over-parametrization === ***

Let us try to provide a high-level explanation. As Subsection 3.2 shows,
the dynamic due to Polyak's momentum has small additive terms cumulated over the iterations, which is due to a fraction of activation pattern could change over iterations and in turn causes some deviation from the accelerated dynamic. Therefore, we want to ensure those undesired terms to be small. By controlling how far the model parameters move away from its initialization, we can control the number of neurons that change the activation during iterations and hence control the total contribution of the deviation to the accelerated dynamic.

Following existing analysis (e.g. (Du et al. 2019b)), Lemma 4 in the appendix shows that $\\| w_t^{(r)} - w_0^{(r)} \\| = \Theta( \eta \sqrt{ \frac{n}{m} }\\| u_0 - y \\| )$, which suggests that the number of neurons $m$ should be a polynomial of $n$ (i.e. the needs for over-parametrization).

*** === Minor === ***

We thank the reviewer for thoroughly reading the paper. We believe the comments have substantially improved this work.

content.title: Review for 'Provable Acceleration of Neural Net Training via Polyak's Momentum'
content.review:
This work studies Polyak’s momentum in neural network training. In detail, the authors show that with sufficient wide two-layer neural network, the use of Polyak’s momentum can accelerate the convergence for the loss to achieve zero loss from $(1-\eta\lambda)^t$ to $(1-\sqrt{\eta\lambda})^t$. The main idea of the proof is to use the fact that the activation patterns during neural network training will not change dramatically from neural tangent kernel (NTK) literature. 

Here are my detailed comments.
- The main contribution of this work is to show Polyak’s momentum accelerates neural network training in the NTK regime. Although the authors claim that such an accelerated convergence rate is nontrivial, I still feel that it is pretty straightforward to obtain this result, given our understanding of NTK. Basically, NTK theory suggests that under the initialization scheme adopted in this work, a wide enough two-layer neural network can be regarded nearly as an overparameterized linear function in terms of the network parameter. Therefore, by adapting the existing results (Eq 6 and (Liu and Belkin, 2020)) about acceleration over an overparameterized linear system brought by momentum-based algorithms, we can directly conclude that the acceleration happens over overparameterized neural networks. To highlight the novelty of this work, the authors may want to highlight the technique difficulties among their proof, and demonstrate the key difference between an overparameterized two-layer neural network and an overparameterized linear system. 
- The authors suggest that by setting $\eta = O(\lambda/n^2)$, the convergence rate of Polyak’s momentum is $(1-\lambda/n)^t$, which is faster than that $(1-\lambda^2/n^2)^t$ of vanilla GD proposed in (Du et al., 2019b). However, (Wu et al., 2019a) suggests that the convergence rate of vanilla GD actually can be improved to $(1-\lambda/\|H^\infty\|_2)^t$, where $H$ is the Gram matrix defined in (3). With the fact that $\|H^\infty\|_2 \leq n$, the convergence rate of vanilla GD is actually $(1-\lambda/n)^t$, the same as that of Polyak’s momentum proposed in this work. Therefore, it seems that Polyak’s momentum does not offer any advantages compared with vanilla GD. 
- Currently, this work does not have any experiments, and it is only for two-layer neural networks. Both of them limit the significance of this work. The authors may want to add some experiments and theoretical analysis for multi-layer neural networks to strengthen their work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
===   **1. Comparison to (Liu and Belkin, 2020, "Accelerating SGD with momentum for over-parameterized learning'')** ===


We appreciate that you drew a connection to the work of Liu and Belkin, 2020. But we want to emphasize that the their setting is quite different from ours. They focus on classical linear regression, i.e. a single neuron with no activation.

$
F(w) := \frac{1}{2} \sum_i ( w^\top x_i - y_i)^2,
$

whereas our setting is about training a one-layer ReLU network with $m$ number of neurons,

$
L(W):= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(  y_i -   N_W(x_i)    \big)^2,
$

where $N_W$ stands for a one-layer ReLU network,
$
N_W := \frac{1}{\sqrt{m} } \sum_{r=1}^m a_r ReLU( \langle w^{(r)},  x \rangle ).
$


Also, it should be noted that the result of (Liu and Belkin 2020) requires that the underlying problem is smooth (Lipschitzness of gradient), and this does not hold for the ReLU activation in our work. Most notably, their analysis requires the underlying function to be convex, while the optimization problem in our setting is non-convex.

We note that there are some negative results of Polyak's momentum in the literature, as we mentioned in the related works. For example, (Lessard et al. 2016) construct a function that is strongly convex but not twice differentiable for which gradient descent with Polyak's momentum fails to converge. We are not aware of any theoretical result for which Polyak's momentum exhibits an acceleration effect, relative to vanilla gradient descent, in non-smooth and non-convex optimization problems. It will be helpful if the reviewer can elaborate on why "one can directly conclude that the acceleration happens" from Liu and Belkin.

While the term over-parameterization does indeed appear in Liu and Belkin, it seems to have been mentioned in order to justify the validity of certain critical assumptions. For example, one of them is (5) in their paper,

$
Var( \hat{\nabla} F(w) ) \preceq \| w - w_* \|^2 E[ \hat{\nabla}^2 F(w) - \nabla^2 F(w)]
$

where $Var( \hat{\nabla} F(w) )$ stands for the variance of stochastic gradient 
$\hat{\nabla} F(w)$, $\hat{\nabla}^2 F(w) $ is the stochastic Hessian and 
$\nabla^2 F(w) $ is the deterministic Hessian.  
This assumption is not nearly relevant to our result, as our convergence rate is for a deterministic algorithm.


We also want to point out that (Kidambi et al. 2018) use the classical linear regression problem to show that SGD with Polyak's momentum fails to achieve an accelerated rate. We also want to note that prior to our work, there is only an asymptotic convergence result regarding Polyak's momentum (Krichene et al., 2020) under the mean-field limit for a one-layer network. 

We would like to note, however, that the reviewer's comments did help bring our attention to two related papers with a similar set of authors (see below). These works do show some interesting theoretical results regarding the optimization landscape, but again we'd like to emphasize that they require the activation to be smooth and are thus not applicable to ReLU.

-- Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, Mikhail Belkin. "Toward a theory of optimization for over-parameterized systems of non-linear equations: the lessons of deep learning." arXiv:2003.00307. 2020

-- Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, Mikhail Belkin. "On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant." arXiv:2010.01092. 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
*** 2. === difference between training an over-parametrized one-layer ReLU network in the NTK regime and solving a system of linear equations === ***

The reviewer suggested that "the authors may want to highlight the technique difficulties among their proof, and demonstrate the key difference between an over-parameterized two-layer neural network and an over-parameterized linear system.'' We emphasize that, in section 3.2, we provide a high-level intuition of our theoretical result, where we have shown the difference between training an over-parametrized one-layer ReLU network in the NTK regime and solving a system of linear equations. However, let us give a brief recap here to see if this helps to elucidate the points.

First, solving a system of linear equations (i.e. $F(w) := \frac{1}{2} \sum_i ( w^\top x_i - y_i)^2$), can be rewritten as a quadratic problem which we described in subsection 2.1,

$
\min_{w \in R^d} \frac{1}{2} w^\top A w + b^\top w,
$

where $A \in R^{d \times d}$ is a symmetric matrix and $b \in R^d$ is a vector. To see this, let the data matrix $X := [x_1; x_2; \dots; x_n]  \in R^{n \times d}$ and the corresponding vector $y:= [y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n]^\top \in R^n$. We have 

$F(w):=\frac{1}{2} \sum_i ( w^\top x_i - y_i)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \\| X w - y \\|^2 = \frac{1}{2} w^\top X^\top X w - y^\top X w + \frac{1}{2} \\| y \\|^2$.


If the matrix $A:= X^\top X \in R^{d\times d}$ turns out to be positive definite, then the problem is a strongly convex quadratic problem, for which Polyak's momentum is known to achieve convergence.
In this case, let $w_* := A^{-1} b$, then it is easy to show that the dynamic of gradient descent with Polyak's momentum evolves as

$
w_{t+1} - w_* = (I_n - \eta A) (w_{t} - w_*) + \beta (w_{t} - w_*) - \beta ( w_{t-1} - w_* ),
$

which can be rewritten as

$
\begin{bmatrix}
w_{t+1} - w_* \\\\\
w_{t} - w_*
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
I_n - \eta A + \beta I_n &  - \beta I_n \\\\\
I_n                      &  0_n
\end{bmatrix}
\cdot
 \begin{bmatrix}
w_{t} - w_*  \\\\\
w_{t-1} - w_* 
\end{bmatrix}.
$

On the other hand, denote $\xi \in R^n$ whose $i_{th}$ entry is $\xi_t[i] := u_t[i] - y[i]$, where $u_t[i]$ is the network prediction $N_t(x_i)$ at time $t$ and $y[i]$ is the true label of sample $i$. Then, in subsection 3.2, we show that under over-parametrization, the dynamic of residual error vector $\xi$ is similar to the above dynamic, modulo some additive terms that need to be carefully controlled.  Specifically, the recursive dynamic is

$
\begin{bmatrix}
\xi_{t+1} \\\\\
\xi_{t} 
\end{bmatrix}
= 
\begin{bmatrix}
I_n - \eta H_t + \beta I_n &  - \beta I_n \\\\\
I_n                   &   0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\xi_{t} \\\\\
\xi_{t-1} 
\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
\phi_t \\\\\ 0
\end{bmatrix},
$

where $H_t \in R^{n \times n}$ is a time-varying Gram matrix and $\phi_t \in R^n$ is a vector whose $i_{th}$ entry satisfies
$|\phi_t[i]| \leq \frac{ 2 \eta \sqrt{n} |S_i^\perp|}{ m } \big(  \\| u_t - y \\| + \beta \sum_{s=0}^{t-1} \beta^{t-1-s}  \\| u_s - y \\| \big).$ To get the recursive dynamic and the bound of each element of $|\phi_t[i]|$ requires careful treatment (e.g. decomposing the prediction dynamics due to momentum into several terms and carefully bounding each term), as the long proof of Lemma 1 in the appendix shows.

The additional technical contribution to ensure that an accelerated rate is achievable in the NTK regime was significant and, we believe, particularly surprising. We required a number of subtle techniques in order to achieve the final result. 

We also want to note that in the classical example of Polyak's momentum (Subsection 2.1),  the dynamic is about the difference between the model parameters, whereas, in the NTK setting, the dynamic is about the residual error. Analyzing how the predictions of the neural network evolve over iterations is typical in the NTK analysis (e.g. Du et al. 2019).

We would like to note, however, that the reviewer's comments did help bring our attention to two related papers with a similar set of authors (see below). These works do show some interesting theoretical results regarding the optimization landscape, but we'd like to emphasize that they require the activation to be smooth and are thus not applicable to ReLU.

-- Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, Mikhail Belkin. "Toward a theory of optimization for over-parameterized systems of non-linear equations: the lessons of deep learning." arXiv:2003.00307. 2020

-- Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, Mikhail Belkin. "On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant." arXiv:2010.01092. 2020.

display_title: new response to Reviewer 4  : about (Liu, Zhu, and Belkin 2020)

content.title: new response to Reviewer 4  : about (Liu, Zhu, and Belkin 2020)
content.comment:
After carefully reading the comment and the papers of Liu, Zhu, and Belkin, we realize that it might be possible that the reviewer was actually referring to the following paper:

--- ''Chaoyue Liu, Libin Zhu, Mikhail Belkin. Toward a theory of optimization for over-parameterized systems of non-linear equations: the lessons of deep learning. arXiv:2003.00307. 2020'',

which was not in our attention but it is now mentioned and discussed in the updated paper.

Indeed, (Liu, Zhu, and Belkin) establish a very interesting connection between solving an over-parametrized non-linear system of equations and solving the classical linear system. Drawn from the connection, they show that for **smooth** and **twice differentiable** activation, the optimization landscape of an over-parametrized network satisfies a notion called Polyak-Lokasiewicz **(PL)** condition:

$
\frac{1}{2} \\| \nabla L(w) \\|^2 \geq \mu ( L(w) - L(w_*)),
$

where $w_*$ is a global minimizer and $\mu > 0$.  However, it is not very clear if their result can be extended to ReLU.  (Safran, Yehudai, and Shamir 2020) show that for a one-layer ReLU network in the student-teacher setting, the PL condition does not hold even locally after any degree of over-parametrization of the student network. Furthermore, to our knowledge, there is little theoretical result of Polyak's momentum showing an accelerated rate when an optimization landscape satisfies the PL condition but has more than one global minimum. On the other hand, for a problem that satisfies PL and has a unique global minimizer, (Aujol et al. 2020) show a variant of Polyak's momentum method having an accelerated rate in a continuous-time limit. So it is not clear if the result is applicable to our setting.

We thank the reviewer for the critical concern. We have added this discussion in the paper. We find the comment very helpful and we believe it substantially helps the presentation of our work.


Ref: 

[1] Itay Safran, Gilad Yehudai, Ohad Shamir. ``The Effects of Mild Over-parameterization on the Optimization Landscape of Shallow ReLU Neural Networks.'' arXiv:2006.01005 2020. 

[2] Jean-Francois Aujol, Charles Dossal, Aude Rondepierre. ``Convergence rates of the Heavy-Ball method with Lojasiewicz property''. hal-02928958. 2020

=== post edit ===

Reviewer 1 has a similar concern. The following is our response:

Our analysis does not follow (Liu et al. 2020a), as it requires smooth and twice differentiable activation and that their results build heavily on characterizing the spectral norm of the Hessian. Also, existing Polyak's acceleration results focus on analyzing the distance between $\\| w_t - w_* \\|$, where $w_*$ is the unique global minimizer of the underlying problem. However, analyzing the distance becomes tricky in our problem. It is not clear if one can show the Hessian of the over-parametrized ReLU network $W_t$ is actually positive definite (as the matrix $A$ on (5) in the paper) nor even properly define it. It is neither clear if the update of Polyak's momentum for the over-parametrized ReLU, $W_t \in R^{d \times m}$, can be well written as the form (5). We neither know which point the update will converge to.

To avoid these difficulties, our analysis focuses on analyzing how the predictions due to Polyak's momentum evolve over time, which is new compared to the existing analysis of Polyak's momentum.
We have to carefully decompose the dynamic of the network's predictions due to momentum. As the dynamic is more complicated than that of vanilla GD, we have to switch back and forth the two equivalent presentations of gradient descent with Polyak's momentum to simplify the analysis.
With this subtle effort, we were able to establish the acceleration result, which was lacking in the literature.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
*** === 3. Comparison to (Wu et al., 2019b) === ***

The reviewer mentions a reference to 
--- Wu et al., 2019a  ("Learning distributions generated by one-layer relu network'' by Wu, Dimakis, Sanghavi.). 
However, since the algorithm proposed by Wu et a. 2019a is not really gradient descent, we presume that the intended reference is 

--- Wu et al., 2019b ("Global convergence of adaptive gradient methods for an over-parameterized neural network'' Wu, Du, Ward; arXiv:1902.07111)

The observation made by the reviewer, that one can improve the bound of Du et al. 2019 with a larger step-size, is very pertinent and indeed helps to improve our result significantly. We sincerely appreciate this observation, and let us describe how we incorporate this in the following. Before that, we want to emphasize that the change we made in the analysis is minimal, as we only had to improve the theorem statement and edit one line in the main proof of the theorem. Kindly find the minor additions in our updated paper.

Let us briefly summarize the result of (Wu et al., 2019b) by using our notation in the paper. Denote $\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H})$ the maximum eigenvalue of the Gram matrix $\bar{H}$ and recall we denote $\lambda:= \lambda_{\min}(\bar{H})$.
Page 20 in (Wu et al., 2019b) shows that by setting the step size $ \eta = \frac{1}{ 2c_0 \lambda_{\max} },$ where the quantity $c_0$ is defined as $ c_0:=\frac 1 {c_1  \lambda_{\max}(\bar{H})} \left(\frac{ (\lambda \delta + 2 n^{3/2} R + n^2 R) (\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H}) + \frac{4n^2R}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \delta}) }{ \lambda \delta} + c_2\right),$ where the quantities $c_1,c_2$ satisfy $1\geq c_1>0$ and  $c_2 > 0$. Wu et al., 2019b show that vanilla gradient with this step size leads to

$
\\| u_t - y \\|^2 = \left( 1 - \frac{c_1 \lambda_{\min} }{c_0 \lambda_{\max} }  \right) \\| u_0 - y \\|^2.
$

Note that $c_0$ is not a universal constant, it depends on the problem parameters $\lambda_{\min}$, $\lambda_{\max}$, $\delta$, and $n$.


With this in mind, we came to realize that our result does not require the step size $\eta$ to be $\eta = O(\frac{\lambda}{n^2})$ as in Du et al. 2019b. Our step size can be as large as

$
\eta = \frac{1}{2 \lambda_{\max}(\bar{H} )},
$

without hurting the analysis.

Let us denote the condition number of the Gram matrix $\bar{H}$ as $\kappa := \frac{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{H}) }{ \lambda_{\min}(\bar{H}) }$.
By using the large step size $\eta = 1 / (2 \lambda_{\max} (\bar{H}) )$,
we show that with the help of momentum, the error decays at the rate

$\left( 1 - \sqrt{ \frac{\eta \lambda_{\min}}{2} }  \right) = \left( 1 - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\kappa}}  \right).$

We believe this is quite an interesting improvement for the following reason: the rate $\left( 1 - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\kappa}}  \right)$ matches that of the accelerated rate for optimizing strongly convex smooth problems (e.g. Nesteorv 1983;2004), and in this case the accelerated rate has an optimal dependency on the condition number $\sqrt{\kappa}$ instead of $\kappa$.
The result should show the clear advantage of the use of Polyak's momentum,
since the result of (Wu et al. 2019b) is 
$  \left( 1 - \frac{c_1}{c_0 \kappa} \right)$.

We really appreciate the reviewer for raising this important concern and we believe the insight of the reviewer has substantially improved this paper.

*** === 4. "add theoretical analysis for multi-layer neural networks'' === ***

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion of considering multi-layer neural networks.
However, the extension should be more appropriate as a separate work. 
We note that (Du et al. ICML 2019) extended the work of (Du et al. ICLR 2019) to a multi-layer setting and that is a 45-page paper. 

To our knowledge, there has not yet been any acceleration result of Polyak's momentum even for the one-layer ReLU network in the NTK regime. As we mentioned in the introduction, prior to our work, there is only an asymptotic convergence result regarding Polyak's momentum (Krichene et al., 2020) under the mean-field limit for a one-layer network.

Ref:

[1]
Gradient Descent Finds Global Minima of Deep Neural Networks
Simon S. Du, Jason D. Lee, Haochuan Li, Liwei Wang, Xiyu Zhai. ICML 2019.

[2]
Gradient Descent Provably Optimizes Over-parameterized Neural Networks
Simon S. Du, Xiyu Zhai, Barnabas Poczos, Aarti Singh. ICLR 2019

*** === 5. "add experiment'' === ***

We plan to add a proof-of-concept experiment in a future version.

content.title: Reviewer 2
content.review:
The paper shows the combined benefits of Polyak’s momentum with overparameterization in single-layer ReLU networks with finite-sum squared-loss.  Notably, the paper shows that momentum achieves an accelerated rate with an error controlled by the number of neurons and samples.
 
 
Strengths:
 
It was not clear why momentum helped with neural network training, and this paper helps to shed light on that.
 
The related work is well-done and places the paper in the literature.
 
The writing in Section 1,2, and 4 is clear.
 
 
Weaknesses:
 
There is no experimental validation for the theory.
 
Section 3.2 to the conclusion is dense and difficult to parse.
 
 
My recommendation is to accept the paper with a 6, but I am not too familiar with work on overparameterization and I was unable to check the details of the proofs.  As such, my confidence is a 2. The paper shows reasoning why momentum may help training deep neural networks in the NTK regime, which may prove useful. However, no experimental results were presented to validate their results.
 
 
The following comments do not affect my score but may help improve the paper:
 
“With infinite number of neurons” -> “with an infinite number of neurons”
 
“Does not explain faster conference of momentum” -> “does not explain the faster convergence of momentum”
 
“Discrete time” -> “discrete-time”, “best known” -> “best-known”, “second order” -> “second-order”, “continuous time” -> “continuous-time”, “mean field” -> “mean-field”
 
“Produce exact same iterates” -> “produce the exact same iterates”
 
“An resemblance” -> “a resemblance”
 
“While obtain the same convergence” -> “while obtaining the same convergence”

“We plot function value of” -> “we plot the function value of”
 
“Provided the weights of neural net” -> “provided the weights of the neural net”
 
There are also various other grammatical points that could be easily fixed by passing the document through an automatic tool.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.comment: We thank you for thoroughly reading the paper and for the positive review. We have updated the paper accordingly and we will make a careful pass on the paper. We plan to add a proof-of-concept experiment in a future version.
